chapter: Boyhood in Evergreen and Calhoun school
title: Music background at Calhoun; the instruments owned by McDowell
summary: His cousin's husband, a Hampton-trained clarinetist, made music strong there; he left his borrowed Evergreen horn, owned by the baseball-team owner who owned all the instruments.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: How much music did you get there?

Well, I got quite a bit because my cousin, she married the professor of Hampton Institute when he came there. He was quite a musician. He was -- had been in the First World War and playing clarinet, and he got his musical education from Hampden.
We're now past the First World War now, huh? We're into what, like 1920's?
Yeah, well, yeah. Yeah, because I entered -- what -- school in 1919? 1918? Yeah. And I came out in '23, something, yeah, '23. And by me playing trumpet

when I went there, it helped to encourage the group. In fact they didn't have a band. And I was so lonesome after I got there because the horn that I was playing in Evergreen wasn't mine, which means I had to leave it.
Oh, I see. Who did it belong to?
Well, it belonged to - - the man who owned the baseball team. He owned everything.
Well, he owned all the instruments.
Oh, I see. He owned the whole --

Yeah, because the band that my brother and father in law played, they got the instruments for these guys, and they could use them here and there, you know, as they wished. And what a ball team they had. Oh, man, it was quite something. And I used to play drums, snare drum, marching around advertising the baseball game, and they give us free tickets, you know.
